condition: where banks keep their head offices

condition: whether electronic funds transfer is an accepted means of payment
state: accepted (وسيلة مقبولة لإجراء الدفع)

condition: legal effect of electronic contracts, records and signatures
state: same legal effect as written documents and signatures

condition: whether offer and acceptance may be made by electronic message
state: an information message is a legally accepted way to make an offer or acceptance

condition: who may operate ATMs

condition: duties of institutions providing electronic funds transfer

condition: payer's liability for unauthorized electronic debits
state: not liable for unauthorized debits made after notifying the bank or institution; liable where his own negligence mainly contributed and the bank did its duties

condition: who approves electronic payment means

condition: who may issue electronic-signature certificates or provide electronic-signature services

condition: general sales tax rate on goods and services sold

condition: annual sales above which a seller must register for sales tax

condition: how often a registered seller must file a sales tax return
state: for every tax period, within 21 days after the end of the previous month, whether or not tax is due
note: Law No. 42 of 2005, Art. 13.

condition: services exempt from sales tax
state: financial and banking services; insurance; health; education; non-profit NGO services; some domestic land transport; residential letting; water, sewerage and electricity; cleaning; restoration of monuments; pilgrimage agencies; hotels of one star or less

condition: goods exempt from sales tax

condition: sales tax rate on exported goods and services
note: Law No. 42 of 2005, Schedule 2 (lines 376-411), which also zero-rates international transport and port services and infant milk.

condition: sales tax rates on specific goods and services

condition: when sales tax on imported goods is paid
state: before release from customs, except production inputs and capital goods of registered manufacturers who keep regular records
note: Law No. 42 of 2005, Art. 34(a).

condition: how sales tax on qat is collected
state: tax officials collect it in qat markets, at city entrances or places the Tax Authority sets, outside registration, returns and invoices; collection by farming-out (القبالة) or contracting is banned

state: old-edition notes only (الدفع بالعملة القديمة فقط)
note: The Dakhm online store's own payment page; it delivers with cash on delivery inside Sana'a (line 14).

condition: whether buyers can pay cash on delivery
state: available inside Sana'a (Dakhm store)
note: The store's own page.

condition: whether buyers can pay online sellers by bank transfer
state: yes: to the store's Al-Kuraimi 'Yemeni account' and 'Saudi account' (الحساب اليمني، الحساب السعودي) or its Haseb point
note: The Dakhm store's own payment page.

condition: whether buyers can pay with a mobile e-wallet
state: available: Jaib, Jawali or Cash, to the store's number
note: The Dakhm store's own payment page.

condition: whether buyers can pay online sellers by transfer through an exchange company
state: available: through Al-Hazmi, Al-Muheet, Al-Najm or Al-Imtiaz, to the named owner
note: The Dakhm store's own payment page.

condition: how buyers prove payment to online sellers
state: by sending a photo of the payment notice on WhatsApp
note: The Dakhm store's own payment page.

condition: whether parties pay for imports in cryptocurrency
state: a Houthi procurement network used Tron wallets, active since 2023 and transacting mostly in Tether's USDT (up to $1 million at a time), to buy commodities from Russia for shipment to Houthi-controlled Yemen
note: OFAC added eight such wallet addresses to its SDN list (line 960), barring U.S. persons from dealing with them.

condition: how remittances from abroad can reach Yemen
state: in stablecoins (USDC or USDT) through Digibank: converted in the app and paid out at over 1,000 liquidity points in Sana'a, Taiz and Aden, for fees of 0.5-2%, in one hour to one day
note: Digibank's own knowledge-base page, marked as edited 24 April 2025 (line 22); some steps on the page name Syrian pounds and the Sham Cash wallet (lines 142, 152, 158).

condition: fee for sending remittances to Yemen
state: 5-8% through traditional banks (3-15 days), 5-10% through Western Union (3-7 days), 5-12% through informal remittance offices (1-2 days)
note: Digibank's comparison table; it calls informal offices illegal with security risks, and says banks and Western Union are limited by sanctions.

condition: whether Western Union pays out in Yemen
state: yes, but limited to the cities by cash shortages and sanctions
note: Digibank's FAQ; the comparison table (line 185) says limited to the major cities.

condition: whether sending money to Yemen is lawful under US rules
state: personal or humanitarian transfers are allowed as long as the recipient is not on international sanctions lists
note: As Digibank's FAQ states the US Treasury rules.

condition: whether buyers rely on cash
state: most economic activity is conducted in cash, from day-to-day purchases to large-scale transactions
note: World Bank, Yemen Financial Sector Diagnostics, dated April 5, 2024 (line 42).

condition: whether one central bank and one currency serve the whole country
state: no: two central banks, in Aden (internationally recognized) and in Sana'a (Houthi-controlled), with inconsistent rules; two currencies in circulation, only one accepted across the country
note: World Bank, Yemen Financial Sector Diagnostics, dated April 5, 2024 (line 42).

condition: which central bank's rules banks follow
state: financial institutions with nationwide operations are subject to the authority of both central banks

condition: where formal banking services are available
state: largely restricted to major cities; rural and remote areas mainly served by money exchangers; 6.3% of adults have access to financial service points and there are 1.6 bank branches per 100,000 adults

condition: whether nonbank lenders are regulated
state: nonbank financial institutions provide credit but are regulated lightly if at all

condition: share of people with a bank account
state: almost entirely unbanked: about 90% of men and 99% of women; 4.8% of adults have deposits and 1.6% borrow from formal institutions
note: Footnote 2 gives the Central Bank of Yemen-Aden as source.

condition: whether depositors can draw their bank deposits
state: many banks froze some or all of their customers' deposits during the liquidity crisis
note: Same sentence: money exchangers let firms keep making international transfers for trade and households receive remittances.

condition: which rial banknotes may be used
state: transactions in notes minted after 2016 prohibited by the central bank in Sana'a
note: The source names only the authority.

condition: whether depositors can draw their bank deposits
state: commercial banks' deposits made before the central banks split remain frozen, and payments on domestic debt are suspended
note: Stated in the report's recommendation that these practices end.

condition: who provides payment services
state: mainly banks and money exchangers; the Yemen Post and Postal Savings Authority and the Postal Savings Fund also provide payment services and savings accounts
note: The sentence continues: 'services, savings accounts, and other financial products' (line 557). Insurance companies and pension funds play only a marginal role.

condition: who performs banking tasks
state: money exchangers: the primary destination for deposits and the main source of credit for traders, providing services such as trade financing once offered by banks
note: Lines 571-572: they serve a much larger share of the population than Yemeni banks.

condition: whether banks may deal in interest
state: a Houthi anti-usury law, in effect since early 2023 and partly implemented, makes banks switch interest-bearing accounts to checking accounts
note: The source names only the authority.

condition: who licenses and supervises banks and money exchangers
state: the Central Bank of Yemen in Aden, which also determines the exchange rate in consultation with the government
note: Under Law 14 of 2000 on the Central Bank (lines 905-911); most of the framework predates the conflict.

condition: which central bank's rules banks follow
state: both the central bank in Aden and the one in Sana'a supervise banks; banks headquartered in the Sana'a region report their financials to Aden, while the two banks' conflicting requirements persist

condition: whether financial consumers are protected by rules
state: the Central Bank in Aden issued a consumer protection regulation in 2023
note: Footnote 9.

condition: which laws govern banking and money exchange
state: Banking Law 38 of 1998; Islamic banks Law 21 of 1996 (amended by Law 16 of 2009); AML/CFT Law 1 of 2010 (amended by Law 17 of 2013); microfinance banks Law 15 of 2009; deposit insurance Law 21 of 2008; money exchange Law 19 of 1995 (amended by Law 15 of 1996); payment systems Law 40 of 2006; financing leases Law 11 of 2007

condition: how the central bank sells foreign currency
state: through a foreign exchange auction system introduced in November 2021, supplying foreign currency particularly for essential imports such as food and fuel
note: Introduced by the Central Bank in Aden.

condition: whether exchange companies may open accounts and take deposits
state: no: regulation prohibits any non-banking institution from accepting deposits; some large exchangers that took deposits are applying for banking licences
note: Lines 1145-1146: money exchangers are also subject to a new framework monitoring capital adequacy, liquidity and profitability.

condition: where merchants and households keep their savings
state: large money exchangers increasingly take deposits from the population
note: Same paragraph: currency outside banks rose from 44% of broad money in 2015 to 48% in 2022.

condition: whether banks and money exchangers must have audited financial statements
state: yes: the central bank in Aden requires financial statements audited by an independent auditor
note: Box 2.

condition: which rial banknotes may be used
state: notes printed by the Aden central bank after the 2016 split banned by the central bank in Sana'a: restrictions from 2017 (banks, exchange companies and traders barred from using them, sometimes confiscated), official ban from December 2019
note: The source calls the Houthis the De-Facto Authority, DFA (lines 473, 796), and places the ban's effects in DFA-controlled regions (line 1289).

condition: whether rial banknotes are in short supply
state: a liquidity shortage, as the pre-2016 notes in circulation deteriorate and cannot be replaced

condition: whether depositors can draw their bank deposits
state: withdrawals allowed on cash deposits made after September 2016; partly restricted on earlier deposits
note: Decision of the central bank in Aden; the source says the decisions of both central banks de facto froze most cash deposits made before the 2016 split (line 1428).

condition: whether depositors can draw their bank deposits
state: withdrawals allowed only on cash deposits accumulated since 2017
note: Decision of the central bank in Sana'a.

condition: what banks must do to keep access to international payments
state: implement SWIFT Scope, which the central bank in Aden mandated for all banks at the end of 2022; most major banks complied, with the Sana'a central bank's approval
note: Box 3; lines 1463-1465: banks that did not would have been cut off from the global financial system and trade finance.

condition: how the central bank sells foreign currency
state: weekly auctions, mainly funded from oil export revenue, in which banks bid volume and price for themselves or their clients; US$15 million a week at first, US$30 million from mid-2022
note: Weekly FX auctions run by the central bank in Aden since November 2021 (line 1707).

condition: how the central bank sells foreign currency
state: a US$2 billion line-of-credit facility funded by Saudi Arabia, giving banks and their clients hard currency to import five key commodities; banks had to deposit cash in Aden to use it
note: In use from 2018 to 2021 (Figure 16), then replaced by the FX auctions.

condition: whether rial cash may be moved between areas
state: physical transfers of pre-2016 rials to the south banned by the central bank in Sana'a
note: Stated as an obstacle for Sana'a banks to the line-of-credit facility.

condition: where formal banking services are available
state: access very limited, especially in rural and conflict-affected areas; people without access, or who distrust banks, rely on informal mechanisms

condition: what services banks mainly offer
state: foreign currency management, mainly money transfers for humanitarian actors and large private importers, and letters of credit, rather than lending and deposit-taking

condition: whether firms can get bank credit
state: very little: private credit fell from 9% of GDP in 2008 to 2% in 2021, and private-sector loans from 30% of bank loans in 2013 to 15% in 2020

condition: how many banks operate
state: 17 traditional banks (13 Yemeni, of which 3 state-owned and 10 private, and 4 foreign-owned) and 9 microfinance banks
note: As of the end of 2023; Table 2 (lines 2316-2351) lists them, source Central Bank of Yemen - Aden.

condition: who may obtain an exchange company licence
state: new licences limited where exchange shops are already concentrated, and minimum initial capital raised
note: Governor's decision No. 4 of 1444H of the central bank in Sana'a on initial capital (footnote 30); lines 2363-2364: the minimum initial capital was increased.

condition: whether banks may deal in interest
state: a law passed by the DFA legislature in March 2023 bans commercial and Islamic banks from lending at high interest rates; the source says it also bans murabaha; its application is ambiguous
note: DFA is the source's name for the Houthi de facto authority (line 796); the source names only the authority.

condition: whether authorities confiscate merchants' property and bank accounts
state: the Public Prosecutor's Office ordered Tadhamon Bank to seize 'VIP accounts'; when it refused, the DFA closed its head office for a time and confiscated its IT assets
note: Box 4; the bank's head office is in Sana'a.

condition: whether buyers can pay with a mobile e-wallet
state: available: Tadhamon Bank's e-wallet Mahfathati
note: Box 4.

condition: how remittances from abroad can reach Yemen
state: through bank payment networks such as Tadhamon Pay, used for domestic transfers and remittances from Saudi Arabia
note: Box 4.

condition: who provides payment services
state: money exchangers, whose networks blend formal and informal channels, carry domestic and international payments, including remittances and trade finance, for a fee
note: Lines 3395-3396: they earn revenue from transaction fees.

condition: whether banks can use the SWIFT network
state: CAC Bank's Sana'a branch was disconnected from SWIFT a few months after the bank's head office moved to Aden in October 2018, but kept serving DFA institutions and selected private clients
note: Box 4; line 3275-3276: the head office moved to Aden in October 2018.

condition: whether Yemeni banks have correspondent banking relationships
state: severely restricted, as Yemen's AML/CFT controls cannot be re-evaluated: listed by the FATF since 2010, with no on-site visit possible as of December 2023
note: Box 5.

condition: how many money exchangers operate
state: 96 companies, 233 institutions and 68 agencies registered with the central bank in Aden
note: Official figures as of 2023.

condition: how many money exchangers operate
state: over 170 companies registered with the central bank in Sana'a
note: Official figures as of 2023.

condition: whether the market exchange rate differs from the official rate
state: the market rate, shaped by money exchangers, can diverge significantly from the official rate set by the central bank in Aden
note: Lines 3400-3405: exchangers mainly convert currencies and give individuals and businesses access to cash.

condition: whether money can be moved between areas held by different parties
state: through money exchangers, as banks in the north and south are disconnected

condition: how many money exchangers operate
state: 415, up from 179 in 2014

condition: how many money exchangers operate
state: 91, up from 34 in 2014

condition: what a money exchanger may do under the exchange law
state: with the central bank's permission: buy and sell foreign currency, accept transfers from abroad, buy and sell travellers' and bank cheques, and other approved business; it may not take deposits or offer bank accounts
note: Article 14 of Republican Decree Law No. 19 of 1995, which governs exchange companies (line 3682).

condition: who may obtain an exchange company licence
state: minimum capital for a new exchange company raised, and new branches limited within a given area
note: Recent rules of the central bank in Aden.

condition: who may obtain an exchange company licence
state: regulations against the oversaturation of exchange companies and harmful financial schemes
note: Introduced in the first quarter of 2023.

condition: whether exchange shops are licensed
state: licensed exchange companies fell from 605 in 2014 to 550 in 2017, while about 800 unlicensed companies entered, often working under licensed ones as agents in tiered networks that reach isolated areas

condition: how domestic money transfers can be made
state: all money exchange companies and transfer networks must transfer through the Unified Money Network, set up after a resolution of the central bank in Aden of November 2020
note: Required from February 2024; lines 3727-3728: the network lets the central bank in Aden monitor transfers across north and south.

condition: what exchange companies must do with unclaimed transfers
state: report them to the central bank after two months
note: Box 7, after a list of unclaimed Emtiaz Express transfers leaked in early 2023; the central bank in Sana'a urged networks to build online tools to find transfers by name (lines 3778-3780).

condition: which Yemeni exchange companies are under US sanctions
state: Al-Omgy and Brother Exchanger (listed in 2016, alleged funnelling to AQAP) and Swaid & Sons Exchange (mid-2021, dealings with Iran)
note: US Treasury sanctions list, as the report states it.

condition: how much can be sent per transfer through money exchangers
state: from US$10 to over US$40,000 per transaction, with no limit on the number of transactions a client can make; importers and other businesses use these services instead of banks
note: Box 7.

condition: where importers obtain foreign currency
state: money exchangers, which became a credible alternative to banks for firms needing foreign exchange for trade
note: Same sentence: also for households to send and receive remittances.

condition: how remittances from abroad can reach Yemen
state: through banks, global transfer companies such as Western Union and MoneyGram (the second largest channel, US$1.1 billion inbound in 2022), and local hawala networks
note: Box 8; lines 4413-4414: their advantages are relatively low fees and extensive networks.

condition: currencies of transfers into Yemen through banks
state: mostly US dollars, then Saudi riyals, euros and UAE dirhams; US$4.9 billion in and US$5.6 billion out through banks in 2022
note: Box 8; data from the central bank in Aden.

condition: what money exchangers must report to the central bank
state: monthly data on capitalisation, leverage, profitability, liquidity, exposures and liabilities, used for a risk rating
note: The central bank in Aden's prudential risk-monitoring framework (line 5448).

condition: share of people with a bank account
state: about 8.8% of the population owned an account of any type, including an e-wallet or other digital account
note: From a 2022 study (SMEPS Digital Payments Study, footnote 48); account ownership was 3.7% in 2011 and 6.4% in 2014 (lines 5751-5752).

condition: whether firms can get bank credit
state: 9.5% of firms had a loan or line of credit in 2022 (5.3% in 2013); informal firms mostly borrow from informal sources such as friends, family or money lenders
note: World Bank Enterprise Surveys.

condition: share of firms with a bank account
state: about 58% of formal firms and 18% of informal firms; banks are concentrated in city centres while about 61% of people live in rural areas
note: 2022 Yemen Enterprise Survey.

condition: whether lenders can check borrowers' credit history
state: Yemen scored 0 out of 8 on depth of credit information in the 2019 Doing Business index

condition: cost of bank credit
state: average lending rate as high as 22%, far above regional peers
note: 2013 is the latest data point the report has for Yemen; 19% of firms in 2022 found rates too high (line 6317).

condition: how public employees receive their salaries
state: in cash, from a teller at the spending unit, over the counter at an exchange house or at the post office; no longer into bank accounts
note: Box 10, on payroll in the government's (IRG) areas (line 6481); lines 6448-6451: the central bank in Aden launched a project to pay over 1.6 million state employees into bank accounts.

condition: how many card terminals (POS) merchants have
state: 817 POS devices in 2019, after falling from 1,500 in 2014 to 200 in 2016

condition: how many ATMs are available
state: 6.4 ATMs per 100,000 inhabitants

condition: whether SME loans can be guaranteed
state: the Yemen Loan Guarantee programme, launched in 2017, had issued over 5,700 guarantees worth YER 10.7 billion by 2022; banks are reluctant to offer such guarantees as recovering defaulted loans takes ever longer

condition: which intermediaries firms mainly use
state: exchange companies for 59% of formal firms, commercial banks for only 20%; firms using bank financing fell from 95% in 2013 to 56% in 2022
note: Yemen Enterprise Surveys.

condition: how widely e-wallets are used
state: e-wallets grew in both north and south under the central banks' digital-payment rules; the Sana'a central bank's restriction of printed notes sped up e-money use; about 800,000 people had mobile money accounts in 2020
note: Lines 6626-6628: a 2019 study found 72% of women and 80% of men used mobile banking for bill payments.

condition: whether payment services are regulated
state: yes: payment-system rules issued by the central bank in Aden since 2019 and then by the one in Sana'a, described as on par with developed countries; the infrastructure is what is missing

condition: whether an instant (fast) payment system is available
state: not yet: an automated clearing house and a real-time clearing system are proposed, pending financing
note: Box 11, on the central bank in Aden's plans.

condition: how remittances from abroad can reach Yemen
state: Yemen has joined Buna, the Arab Monetary Fund's platform for remittances and cross-border payments
note: Box 11.

condition: who offers electronic payment services
state: three commercial banks in Aden offered e-wallets as of December 2023; licensing of non-bank payment providers under way, with three in advanced stages and two from Sana'a applying to provide e-wallets in Aden
note: Box 11.

condition: whether payment providers from one area may operate in the other
state: payment providers from Sana'a may not operate in Aden without investing in separate infrastructure located in the south
note: Box 11; same passage: rules and infrastructure are similar in both areas.

condition: whether buyers can pay with the electronic rial
state: the e-rial is used in place of e-wallets, to curb banknote deterioration
note: Box 11, comparing the central bank in Sana'a with the one in Aden.

condition: cost of microfinance credit
state: average interest of 19%
note: Lines 6693-6695: 13 of 15 MFIs are backed by the Social Fund for Development, which lends them capital at 0%.

condition: how much a microfinance bank may lend to one borrower
state: a credit ceiling of US$1,000
note: Same passage: 22 exchange-house groups applied for microfinance bank licences, of which more than 5 were approved by the central bank in Aden.

condition: share of firms with a bank account
state: 63% of formal firms
note: Annex III, 2022 Yemen Enterprise Survey (58% of the 328 formal firms overall).

condition: share of firms with a bank account
state: 54% of formal firms
note: Annex III, 2022 Yemen Enterprise Survey.

condition: what collateral lenders require
state: sometimes worth more than 100% of the loan: land or building deeds of the borrower, personal assets, or gold
note: Annex III, as reported by respondents to the 2022 Yemen Enterprise Survey.

condition: which intermediaries firms mainly use
state: money exchange companies for about 73% of firms, commercial banks for 24%; almost a quarter say they need no financial intermediary
note: Annex III, 2022 Yemen Enterprise Survey (a multiple-option question; the main text gives 59% and 20% for formal firms, line 6620).

condition: rial price of one US dollar
note: Mid-July 2025, before the rial in Aden appreciated sharply in August 2025 (section D, Monetary Policy and Inflation).

condition: rial price of one US dollar
state: about YER 1,600, and has since stabilized; the Aden rial has even appreciated slightly since mid-February
note: From August 2025. Spring 2026 edition: its analysis reflects the situation as of end-March 2026 (lines 173-175); 2026-05 is the PDF's creation date.

condition: whether banks and exchange companies may deal at a rate of their own
state: official rates are enforced (enforced official rates)
note: One of the means by which the rial has been held near YER 535 per US$1; the source does not name who must keep to the official rates.

condition: whether the government controls prices of basic goods
state: price controls
note: One of the means by which the rial has been held near YER 535 per US$1; the source does not name the goods.

condition: rial price of one US dollar
state: near YER 535, held there through constrained money supply, enforced official rates and price controls; the pre-2016 rial has remained trading around YER 535
note: Spring 2026 edition: analysis as of end-March 2026 (lines 173-175); 2026-05 is the PDF's creation date.

condition: whether buyers rely on cash
state: the local economy remains largely cash-based, and liquidity shortages are intensifying
note: Executive summary.

condition: whether depositors can draw their bank deposits
state: cash withdrawal restrictions, amid severe liquidity shortages
note: Same sentence: these compressed household and business spending.

condition: whether firms can get bank credit
state: formal credit largely absent
note: Same sentence: this compressed household and business spending.

condition: whether Yemeni banks have correspondent banking relationships
state: correspondent banking relationships severed, as institutions relocate from Sana'a to Aden amid elevated sanctions risk after the U.S. re-designated the Houthis a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) in early 2025
note: The paragraph begins 'In Houthi-controlled areas' (line 300); the source does not say whose relationships were severed.

condition: where financial institutions are based
state: financial institutions increasingly relocating from Sana'a to Aden amid elevated sanctions risk following the US Foreign Terrorist Organization redesignation of the Houthi movement in early 2025
note: Executive summary ('are increasingly relocating'); the 2025 chapter says the same (lines 309-316).

condition: where formal banking services are available
state: banking activity increasingly concentrated in Aden; populations in Houthi-controlled areas left with even more limited access to formal financial services
note: Same paragraph as the relocation of institutions from Sana'a to Aden (lines 309-316).

condition: whether imports can reach Yemen's ports
state: Israeli airstrikes on Hodeidah port reduced import capacity significantly, tightening the supply of food, fuel and essential commodities; repeated strikes on Hodeida between May and July 2025 reduced port capacity and disrupted operations
note: Imports through Houthi-controlled ports fell in 2025 (lines 692-696: their share of imports 67% in 2025, 75% in 2024).

condition: which goods may not be imported
state: petroleum, via Houthi-held facilities (U.S. restrictions prohibiting petroleum imports, effective April 4, 2025)
note: The source names only the authority (U.S.). It gives this as one cause of the shift of imports away from Houthi-controlled ports in 2025.

condition: whether foreign currency may be used in local transactions
state: no: a ban on using foreign currency in local transactions
note: A measure of the Central Bank of Yemen (CBY) in Aden, which the source says the rial's appreciation in Aden in August 2025 reflects; the source names only the authority. Line 1316 speaks of continued enforcement of CBY-Aden's exchange rate measures.

condition: availability of foreign currency
state: capped (caps on foreign-currency access)
note: A measure of the Central Bank of Yemen (CBY) in Aden, which the source says the rial's appreciation in Aden in August 2025 reflects; the source names only the authority.

condition: which exchange companies may operate

note: A measure of the Central Bank of Yemen (CBY) in Aden, which the source says the rial's appreciation in Aden in August 2025 reflects; the source names only the authority.

condition: how imports are regulated and financed

condition: whether imports can reach Yemen's ports
state: many shipments have failed to reach their destinations: cargo vessels docked at regional hubs (Jeddah, Dubai, Muscat, Djibouti), but the final leg of their journey to IRG-controlled ports remains effectively blocked
note: 'As of early May'; after the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted from March 1 (line 1103-1104), in the 2026 Middle East conflict.

condition: cost of shipping and insuring imports

note: Footnote 11 cites the World Bank's Financial Sector Diagnostic Report for Yemen; the same paragraph (lines 338-340) gives 96 money exchange companies in Aden by 2023.

condition: what a money exchanger may do under the exchange law
state: exchange companies may not perform banking functions such as commercial financial transfers, opening accounts, credit and debit operations, or large-scale currency transactions (Law No. 19 of 1995, Articles 21, 22 and 23)
note: Footnote 12: Law on Foreign Exchange Activities, Republican Decree No. (19) of 1995.

condition: whether exchange companies may open accounts and take deposits
state: the parallel market has surpassed the legal restrictions; its methods have included opening accounts for war profiteers and individuals involved in corruption
note: Lines 631-633: methods by which the parallel market enabled money laundering and illicit financing during the war.

condition: whether one may deal in virtual assets or cryptocurrencies
state: the parallel market has used cryptocurrency trading to obscure the origin of funds
note: Listed among the parallel market's money-laundering methods during the war.

condition: how the central bank sells foreign currency
state: directly to traders, against official import documentation at the CBY exchange rate, to keep essential commodities such as wheat, milk, sugar and medicines available (the 'substitution mechanism'); about USD 1.2 billion in 2016
note: For 2015 to 2016; the source names only the authority (CBY).

condition: whether Yemeni banks have correspondent banking relationships
state: Yemeni banks' U.S. dollar accounts closed by correspondent banks, following U.S. Treasury Department directives, which limited their ability to settle import payments in US dollars
note: Phase One, 2015 to 2019.

condition: currency in which banks settle import payments
state: the euro, despite its higher transaction costs, after correspondent banks closed the banks' U.S. dollar accounts
note: In the Phase One section (2015 to 2019).

condition: where importers obtain foreign currency
state: the parallel market, which became the main source of import financing
note: Phase One, 2015 to 2019.

condition: whether banks can draw their balances at the central bank
state: restricted by the CBY due to the liquidity shortage
note: In the Phase One section (2015 to 2019); same sentence: banks had to meet importers' payment obligations abroad and massive cash withdrawals at home.

condition: how remittances from abroad can reach Yemen
state: a significant portion of external remittances to Yemen began flowing through informal channels
note: In the Phase One section (2015 to 2019), amid the banking liquidity crisis.

condition: whether depositors can draw their bank deposits
state: the business community, its confidence in commercial banks undermined by the liquidity crisis, increased cash withdrawals, and liquidity flowed toward the parallel market
note: In the Phase One section (2015 to 2019).

condition: how remittances from abroad can reach Yemen
state: through informal channels of the parallel market, which exploited restrictions imposed in Saudi Arabia on remittances from expatriates and investors, particularly limits on transferring large amounts directly

condition: how remittances from abroad can reach Yemen
state: a large portion does not pass through banks and is handled by money exchange companies or informal money transfer networks
note: Per an ACAPS report of October 2021, as the source cites it.

condition: where importers obtain foreign currency
state: the parallel market, which finances imports from foreign balances built from expatriate remittances, through covert networks and social-media-based channels outside any formal oversight; used daily for hundreds of transactions
note: Remittances captured particularly in Saudi riyals and US dollars (line 423).

condition: how importers pay foreign suppliers
state: through an exchange company: the trader deposits Yemeni rials locally and the exchanger pays the supplier abroad from its foreign balance through a third party (e.g. a trader in Saudi Arabia or an external account), at its own margin; exchangers use front or proxy accounts of traders in neighbouring countries
note: Example: USD 300,000 to China, sold to the trader at 3.85 SAR per USD while bought at the CBY's official 3.75; lines 525-528: China, India and the UAE accept exports to Yemen invoiced in the name of non-Yemeni companies.

condition: how money transfers can be made
state: through unsupervised individual remittance and exchange networks operating entirely outside the formal regulatory framework, concentrated largely in Sana'a

condition: whether electronic balances trade at par with cash
state: these networks create parallel pricing between cash and electronic balances

condition: how money transfers can be made
state: 64% use the Hawala system as their primary method for transferring money rather than banks; 71% of communities rely on informal exchange outlets
note: Per a World Bank report (footnote 18: Financial Sector Diagnostic Report for Yemen, December 2024).

condition: how domestic money transfers can be made
state: only through the Unified Remittance Network (UNMONEY): Decree No. 23 halted the operations of other bank and exchange company networks, limiting all domestic remittances to the unified network
note: The network, set up by the Aden-CBY under Decree No. 18 of 2020, was officially activated in February 2024.

condition: who takes part in the unified money network (الشبكة الموحدة للأموال)
state: banks relocated to Aden, encouraged by the Aden-CBY to contribute to the network (capital raised to YER 12 billion), with a central role in its management
note: The source names the network the Unified Remittance Network (UNMONEY); footnote 26 cites a Central Bank statement of July 2025.

condition: who may obtain an exchange company licence
state: capital of YER 1 billion for partnership exchange companies, YER 500 million for individual money exchange outlets and YER 100 million for remittance agents
note: Footnote 24: Decision No. 58 of 2022 on Regulating Money Exchange Activities, August 2022. Same paragraph: inspections and field oversight intensified.

condition: what capital a microfinance bank must hold
state: YER 15 billion under Decree 3/2023, raised from YER 5 billion under Decree 11-2-2022, payable 50% a year over two years
note: Same sentence: the Aden-CBY granted new licences to microfinance banks.

condition: whether exchange and microfinance activities may be combined
state: prohibited by the Aden-CBY, although in practice the overlap continued

condition: what capital a bank must hold
state: a minimum of YER 45 billion for operating banks (Decree No. 8/2022 of the Aden-CBY)
note: The source says 'operating banks in Yemen'; footnote 28 dates the decision March 2022.

condition: where banks keep their head offices
state: all commercial, Islamic and microfinance banks operating in Yemen must relocate their headquarters from Sana'a to Aden within 60 days (Decision No. 17 of 2024 of the Aden-CBY), on pain of 'legal measures' under the AML/CFT law; the decision was not implemented immediately
note: The source says 'operating in Yemen'.

condition: what banks must do to keep access to international payments
state: show proof of relocation to Aden: correspondent banks follow the directives of the Aden-CBY, which requested it from financial institutions wishing to continue their international transactions
note: After Decision No. 17 of 2024; banks were also under pressure from the Sana'a branch of the Central Bank, under Houthi control.

condition: rial price of one US dollar
note: Reached before the Central Bank of Yemen in Aden's measures of 2025.

condition: how the central bank oversees exchange companies
state: strict supervision of liquidity flows and of conversions between foreign currencies and the rial, with direct and indirect oversight of the financial systems operated by money exchange companies
note: Among the measures of 2025.

condition: which Yemeni banks are under US sanctions
state: two Yemeni banks, plus several exchange companies and commercial firms, sanctioned by the U.S. Department of the Treasury in January 2025
note: The source does not name the banks.

condition: where banks keep their head offices
state: all major banks and leading exchange companies left Sana'a and moved their headquarters to Aden, making the banking sector fully operational from Aden, according to the Governor of Aden-CBY
note: After the U.S. sanctions of January 2025 and the Houthis' listing as a terrorist-supporting organization (lines 940-955).

condition: which exchange companies may operate
state: licences revoked for exchange companies and establishments that violated regulations, particularly by currency speculation or by breaching operational ceilings and professional standards set by the Aden-CBY
note: Among the measures of 2025.

condition: where importers obtain foreign currency
state: traders rely on the parallel market to access foreign currency, raising prices of essential goods such as food, fuel and medicine
note: Listed among the impacts of the parallel market in Yemen (line 835).

condition: availability of foreign currency
state: severe shortage of foreign cash within the country, from currency smuggling abroad
note: Listed among the impacts of the parallel market in Yemen (line 835).

condition: where importers obtain foreign currency
state: from most incoming foreign currency remittances, which the Houthi group controlled to fund imports
note: Section 'Existing Policies'.

condition: whether banks and exchange companies may deal at a rate of their own
state: the Houthi group fixes the exchange rate and imposes strict oversight over the parallel market
note: Section 'Existing Policies'; the source says this stabilized exchange rates on the surface but contracted economic activity.

condition: whether banks and exchange companies may deal at a rate of their own
state: a floating exchange rate, with weak oversight of the parallel market
note: Section 'Existing Policies'; the same section says the IRG has recently implemented new measures to stop the rial's depreciation and regulate the exchange market (lines 891-894).

condition: how imports are regulated and financed
state: the National Committee for Regulating Imports introduced a clear mechanism for buying and selling foreign currency and for organizing the flow of imports through the customs entry points
place: National Committee for Regulating Imports' area
note: The source names only the committee; it credits the committee foremost for improved exchange-rate stability.

condition: whether exchange shops are licensed
state: the parallel currency market includes unlicensed or non-compliant money exchange companies, as well as currency speculators and war profiteers

condition: which Yemeni banks are under US sanctions
state: International Bank of Yemen (IBY) and three of its top executives, designated for financial support to the Houthis: all property and interests under US jurisdiction blocked, with a higher risk of secondary sanctions for those who continue to deal with it; after the January action against Yemen Kuwait Bank for Trade and Investment
note: Designated 'on Thursday' by the Treasury's OFAC under Executive Order 13224; the article is dated Apr 17, 2025.

condition: where banks keep their head offices
state: IBY, headquartered in Houthi-controlled Sana'a, has refused to relocate its operations from Houthi-held territory despite calls by authorities in Aden
note: Line 41: IBY is headquartered in Houthi-controlled Sana'a.

condition: whether banks can use the SWIFT network
state: IBY, headquartered in Houthi-controlled Sana'a, has allegedly used its SWIFT access to facilitate international transactions for Houthi-affiliated entities, including oil purchases
note: According to OFAC (same paragraph).

condition: whether authorities confiscate merchants' property and bank accounts
state: IBY helped the Houthis confiscate assets from rivals
note: According to OFAC; the source names only the Houthis.

condition: how domestic money transfers can be made
state: the local transfer networks of banks, financial institutions and exchange companies halted completely and permanently, with pending transactions to be settled within fifteen days; violators face licence revocation, cessation of activity and financial penalties
note: Decision of the Central Bank in Aden of Wednesday 26 June; it addresses those 'operating in the Republic'. The page shows Friday, 28 June 2024 (line 13), though the manifest calls it undated.

condition: who takes part in the unified money network (الشبكة الموحدة للأموال)
state: numerous banks and exchange entities; the Central Bank in Aden had directed all commercial banks and exchange companies to engage with it
note: Per journalist Wafaq Saleh (line 54); line 76 says the network was established 'in February of the previous year', line 29 'in February'.

condition: how money transfers can be made
state: mostly through thousands of financial transfer networks, most of them operating outside the central bank's control
note: Per journalist Wafaq Saleh; he says speculators use them to manipulate the rial.

condition: who takes part in the unified money network (الشبكة الموحدة للأموال)
state: dealings with it prevented by the Houthi group
note: Per economic specialist Najib Al-Adofi.

condition: fee for domestic money transfers
state: increased, as the Houthi group imposes the use of two different currencies with varying sizes and values
note: Per economic specialist Najib Al-Adofi.

condition: rial price of one US dollar
state: over YER 1,800, the rial's lowest level
place: Aden and areas under the Yemeni government's control

condition: rial price of one US dollar
place: Aden and areas under the Yemeni government's control
note: The 'late April rate'.

condition: rial price of one Saudi riyal
state: YER 477 selling
place: Aden and areas under the Yemeni government's control

condition: rial price of one Saudi riyal
state: YER 441
place: Aden and areas under the Yemeni government's control
note: 'The previous rate'; the source gives no date for it.

condition: whether rial banknotes are in short supply
state: a severe cash crisis, worsened by the deepening disruption of the local currency
note: Line 70 (Al-Adofi): a liquidity crisis in both local and foreign currencies.

condition: which exchange companies may operate
state: licences of 12 more money exchange companies and establishments suspended (Hawam, Pure Money, Top Top, Al-Sahem Al-Asra', Al-Qasimi Express, Al-Nasseri, Al-Arabi Express, Al-Hadath (transfer agent), Al-Saeed Express, Basma Express, Dawood Al-Amri), for violations confirmed by field inspection; 15 suspended in all
note: Two decisions of the Governor of the Central Bank of Yemen in Aden 'within the past 24 hours'. The page shows Thursday, 04 July 2024 (line 13), though the manifest calls it undated.

condition: which exchange companies may operate
state: licences of three companies suspended: Thamar Exchange, Al-Mari Exchange and its branches, Al-Majrabi Exchange and its branches

condition: how domestic money transfers can be made
state: new local cash transfers by exchange companies, establishments and transfer agents only through the Unified Money Transfer Network (UNMONEY), from the decision date; banks' own networks may run alongside it until 30 July 2024; the local transfer networks of banks, financial institutions and exchange companies to cease completely and permanently
note: Decision of the Central Bank in Aden; the source says the networks are those of institutions 'operating in the country'.

condition: what exchange companies must do with unclaimed transfers
state: report unpaid transfers not yet delivered to their recipients to the Central Bank of Yemen headquarters in Aden, with detailed data, within twenty days
note: Same decision of 26 June 2024 on the local transfer networks; the sentence begins 'Regarding unpaid transfers not yet delivered to their recipients'.

condition: where banks keep their head offices
state: banks operating in Houthi-controlled Sana'a are relocating their headquarters to Aden to avoid U.S. sanctions on the Houthis
note: As the Central Bank of Yemen in Aden announced 'Friday'; after the U.S. designated the Houthis a Foreign Terrorist Organization on March 4, 2025. The page shows Friday, 14 March 2025 (line 13), though the manifest calls it undated.

condition: where banks keep their head offices
state: the Yemeni Bank for Reconstruction and Development moved its headquarters from Houthi-controlled Sana'a to Aden, the ninth bank to follow the Central Bank of Yemen's directives to relocate; eight others had committed to move by 16 March 2025
note: The eight are named at line 25. The Houthi-controlled central bank branch in Sana'a condemned the relocations (line 27).

condition: what banks must do to keep access to international payments
state: comply with the Central Bank in Aden: banks still operating from Sana'a face tightened restrictions on international transactions, and possible freezing of overseas accounts or disconnection from the global financial system, after the U.S. designation of the Houthis effective March 3, 2025
note: The page shows Monday, 14 July 2025 (line 13), though the manifest calls it undated.

condition: whether one may deal with e-wallets the Central Bank in Aden has not licensed
state: prohibited: a circular prohibiting dealing with unlicensed entities, wallets and electronic payment services
note: The Central Bank's own news item (headquarters Aden, lines 11 and 52), dated 2024-06-26 though the manifest calls the page undated; the circular itself is an attached document not captured here.

condition: where banks keep their head offices
state: eight banks headquartered in Sana'a (Tadhamon, Al-Kuraimi Islamic Microfinance, Shamil Bank of Yemen & Bahrain, Islamic Bank of Yemen for Finance and Investment, Saba Islamic, Yemen Gulf, Yemen Commercial, Al-Amal Microfinance) notified the Central Bank of their decision to relocate their headquarters and operations to Aden, to avoid U.S. sanctions; the Central Bank will issue certificates of relocation
note: The Central Bank of Yemen's own announcement (headquarters Aden, line 11), dated 2025-03-15 though the manifest calls the page undated; after the U.S. designation of Ansar Allah (Houthis) as an FTO.

condition: where banks keep their head offices
state: several Yemeni banks headquartered in Sanaa decided to relocate their operations to Aden to avoid U.S. sanctions on the Houthis
note: As the Central Bank of Yemen said on Saturday, March 15, 2025.

condition: which banks the Central Bank in Aden deals with
state: dealings suspended with six major commercial banks, for failing to relocate from Sanaa to Aden and for cooperating with the Houthis
note: 'In May last year'; the article is dated 2025-03-15.

condition: which banks the Central Bank in Aden deals with
state: the May 2024 suspension of dealings with six major commercial banks was canceled following external mediation
note: The source says only 'later' for the cancellation.
